Hey sounds like you've got a lot going on here, thought I might try to chime in with some advice, but please take it with a grain of salt as I haven't been in the veterinary field for over 5 years now.

First thing's first, do you have any other cats at home? Bringing a feral cat into a home where there are existing cats can bring diseases like distemper or calicivirus, even if the cats are kept in separate areas of the house. Just something to keep in mind.

Secondly, you should bring the kitten to a veterinarian, at least for a health exam. They'll also be able to tell you its sex and approximate age, plus give you advice on what to do about the constipation issue.

To determine the kitten's sex yourself, you can use its anogenital distance This article gives a really good explanation with pictures.

Figuring out the kitten's age is another important thing. This page has lots of good information including a visual chart. If I had to guess from your photo, your kitten looks to be around 4 or 5 weeks old, which although the kitten is gaining some independence, still relies on its mom for many things, including voiding (urinating/defecating).

Mother cats help their kittens urinate/deficate by licking their genitals. Obviously you're not gonna do that, but you can take a warm, damp wash cloth and gently rub it over the kitten's genitals to try and stimulate voiding. Usually kitten's don't need help with this after about 3 weeks of age, but since we don't know the age of your kitten, it's worth a try. I noticed you originally posted this about 12 hours ago, so if the kitten still hasn't urinated or defecated by now, call a vet ASAP because this could be an emergency situation.

Another thing that could be causing the constipation is a heavy parasite burden, especially since the kitten is feral. All kitten's have roundworms initially (it's just how the lifecycle of the parasite works, they automatically get them from mom) and there could be so many of them that the kitten is having trouble defecating. You will definitely want to call a vet about getting a dewormer - the over-the-counter stuff you can find at a pet store is a different medication and doesn't usually work too well.

As for feeding, kittens still need milk at this age, though they are starting to explore solid foods as well. You'll need to get a Kitten Milk Replacement (also called KMR) and syringe feed it to the kitten. Your vet will have some, but most pet stores sell it also. You can start introducing the kitten to solid foods (I recommend starting with canned food, then gradually introducing kibble) and the kitten will need less KMR as it gets older because it will start eating more solids. The kitten should still receive KMR until at least 8 weeks of age.

I know this is a lot of info, so don't be afraid to call a vet, shelter, or local rescue for advice. The University of Wisconsin also has a fairly thorough guide here
